author: kevaundray
content:
Currently have an agent extracting the patches from lighthouse into the CL specs to see them a bit better. (It seems like we inspect frame txs on the CL to compute the hashes for the dependencies in the dependency frame, which I think CL devs would not want) 

I would propose the following milestones:

- 1) devnets with just leanSPHINCS no aggregation and we collect metrics on what this looks like. This should mostly be an EL change.

- 2) devnets with block builder aggregation. This is where starkProof in the block would be added. This would probably not help mempool issues that much only block propagation.

- 3a) devnets with leanPCS added. This would further increase the mempool traffic and potentially the compute needed by the builder

- 3b) devnets with mempool aggregation.

3b is massive, though I think <@857052906495017000> has been working on this for a while now?

author: jhon_fp
content:
<@427491045308235776>  On keccak256(stark_proof): with aggregation, individual signatures never go on chain. Each transaction only declares its claim (scheme, digest, public key) in a DEP_VERIFY frame, and the block's STARK proof is the only evidence that those signatures are valid. No other header field covers that proof, so its hash is committed in the EL header, alongside block_deps_hash (the commitment to the claims). This binds the exact proof to the block hash: a block cannot be relayed or rebuilt with a different or missing proof under the same hash. On the devnet, the CL recomputes the block hash, deriving the deps hash from the frame transactions, and rejects any mismatch regardless of the EL's verdict. Engine API: ExecutionPayload only gains starkProof.

Context: https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-8288

This is our reading of the design rationale; <@&652918665943056397> can confirm the original intent.

author: ulisse195
content:
The milestones make sense to us. 
Related to (1), we already run native (non-aggregated) SPHINCS frame accounts on devnet-0: the account contract verifies the signature in its VERIFY frame, with no block proof, and our wallet supports this mode alongside aggregation. This is a contract-level approach rather than EL-native verification, and it still uses the current SPHINCS profile rather than upstream leanSPHINCS, but it can provide early data on signature size and verification cost. 

On (2), we are waiting for <@&652918665943056397> 's  latest leanVM implementation before updating our side, since it changes the aggregation key and requires a new genesis.

To get meaningful metrics for (1) and (2), the network will need sustained load rather than a handful of wallet transactions. I think <@&1416139337179074590> s will cover this in the next steps with a spammer generating frame transactions with leanSPHINCS signatures, which would show how mempool traffic, block propagation and builder compute behave under realistic signature sizes.

author: deanstef
content:
Hey <@427491045308235776> ! Stefano from Nethermind here 🙂

The main rationale for having `hash(proof)` in the block header rather than the full proof was to avoid bloating headers with quite large objects (~300 kB). Think about light clients or nodes fetching block headers during sync: EIP-8288 would have added ~300 kB per header. The hash still commits the block to the exact proof bytes.

- We started the discussion here: https://github.com/ethereum/EIPs/pull/12479, initially proposing to move the proof into the block body while keeping its hash in the header.

- We then converged on the approach in https://github.com/ethereum/EIPs/pull/12549, where proofs are transmitted separately from both headers and bodies. This also allows nodes to fetch and prune proofs independently, without increasing block body sizes.

<@348512261955911691> <@232483425318207488> can add more 🙂
